routes.name: Big Red — Al Badayer
routes.summary: Iconic red-sand dunes minutes from the Dubai–Hatta road. A great first big-dune outing with a wide playground and plenty of escape routes; busy on weekends.
tips: Go early to beat weekend crowds and chewed-up sand.
Descend the big dune straight down the fall line, never sideways.
hazards: Steep slip-face on the main red dune.
Quad/buggy traffic on weekends.

routes.name: Fossil Rock — Maleha
routes.summary: A striking quartzite outcrop rising from the gravel plains, famed for ancient marine fossils embedded in its reddish cliffs. The approach wadi is rocky and requires high ground clearance; the summit rewards with panoramic views across three emirates.
routes.permitInfo: No permit required; respect UAE ecotourism signage.

campingSpots.name: Wadi floor camp
campingSpots.notes: Open flat area before the final climb; good stargazing.

tips: Approach via the main Sharjah–Kalba road (E102), turn off after the Maleha roundabout.
Keep tyres at gravel pressure — the wadi base has sharp limestone shards.
Bring a hat and extra sun protection; there is no shade on the upper section.
hazards: Sharp rock edges can puncture tyres.
Loose scree on the upper approach track.
No mobile signal in the wadi.

routes.name: Liwa — Moreeb Dune
routes.summary: Tal Moreeb — the UAE's tallest dune at ~300 m with a 50-degree slip-face — anchors a vast mega-dune playground on the northern edge of the Empty Quarter. An epic two-day expedition for experienced dune drivers.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 low-range essential; dedicated off-road tyres strongly recommended
routes.permitInfo: None, but inform someone of your itinerary; nearest rescue is hours away.

checklist.item: Dedicated GPS unit with UAE maps

campingSpots.name: Moreeb base camp
campingSpots.notes: Sand flat at the foot of the great dune; shelter from prevailing wind.

campingSpots.name: Northern inter-dune flat
campingSpots.notes: Midway overnight camp; clear desert sky.

tips: Start pre-dawn to reach the dune base in cool air before heat builds.
Approach Moreeb from the north — the south face is a sheer drop into Saudi territory.
Fuel up completely in Liwa town; there are no petrol stations beyond.
hazards: Extreme isolation — rescue response time can exceed 4 hours.
Sand can be deceptively soft; even experienced drivers get stuck.
Heat stroke risk in summer; strictly Oct–Apr only.
Saudi border is nearby — do not cross marked dunes on the south side.

routes.name: Sweihan Desert Crossing
routes.summary: The corridor between Al Ain and Abu Dhabi hides a serious dune belt nicknamed 'Little Liwa'. Large, steep dunes on soft sand make this a demanding proving ground for drivers who've mastered Big Red and want the next challenge.

checklist.item: GPS or offline maps (no signal in parts)

campingSpots.name: Central dune hollow
campingSpots.notes: Sheltered inter-dune flat, good for an overnight before continuing.

tips: Enter from Al Hayer Road and use a GPS track — the area looks uniform and navigation is easy to lose.
Exit via a pre-agreed point; pick-up from a graded road is safest.
Camels roam freely — slow down at dune crests.
hazards: Very large dunes with soft, steep faces.
Limited mobile coverage across much of the crossing.
Camels on dune crests are invisible until you summit.

routes.name: Wadi Showka Loop
routes.summary: A rewarding mountain wadi loop in the Hajar foothills north-west of RAK. Rocky stream bed, acacia-lined banks, and seasonal pools make this a favourite for cooler months. The wadi narrows dramatically in the upper section.

campingSpots.name: Upper wadi pools camp
campingSpots.notes: Near seasonal pools; bring your own water supply regardless.

tips: Visit after winter rain (Jan–Mar) for water in the pools.
The loop's return leg crosses open gravel — watch speed on loose pebbles.
Start early as the wadi can become very warm by midday.
hazards: Flash flooding risk during and after rain — check weather before entry.
Large boulders in the upper narrows require careful line selection.
Track can be slippery when wet.

routes.name: Pink Rock — Al Faya
routes.summary: A photogenic rose-pink quartzite monolith rising from the golden sands of inland Sharjah. The surrounding soft-sand plain is excellent for beginner dune driving, and the rock itself makes a dramatic sunset backdrop for camping.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 recommended; a capable crossover can manage the main access track

campingSpots.name: Pink Rock east face
campingSpots.notes: Sheltered by the rock; stunning sunrise views.

tips: Perfect for a family day trip — dunes are gentle and forgiving.
The '2nd of December' roadside cafe at 25.0411, 55.7321 is a good re-inflate stop.
Sunset here is spectacular — arrive by 4 pm in winter.
hazards: Soft sand beyond the main area can trap light vehicles.
Broken glass near popular camp spots — check before pitching.

routes.name: Hatta Mountain Trail
routes.summary: The rugged wadi and ridge network behind Hatta town offers some of the most technical rocky driving in the Dubai emirate. Tight wadi crossings, steep loose-rock climbs, and stunning mountain panoramas reward prepared crews.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 low-range essential; good skid plates recommended
routes.permitInfo: No permit. Hatta Mountain Conservation Area — stay on marked tracks.

campingSpots.name: Hatta wadi flat
campingSpots.notes: Shaded by acacia trees in the morning; firm gravel base.

tips: Download offline maps before leaving — signal disappears in the upper wadis.
The Hatta Dam is worth a quick stop at the start.
Mechanical recovery can take 2+ hours; tell someone your exit plan.
hazards: Loose rock and scree on steep descents.
Flash floods in the wadi — check weather 24 h in advance.
Very limited phone signal throughout.
routes.attribution: Track approximated from public map data; details curated by TrailPilot

routes.name: Jebel Jais Foothills
routes.summary: The lower flanks of the UAE's highest peak (1934 m) host a network of off-road tracks through dramatic gorges and ancient wadis. The Wadi Qadaah route is a classic: a narrow canyon, sheer limestone walls, and cool mountain air.
routes.permitInfo: No formal permit; Jebel Jais summit road access may require RAK municipality pass for some tracks.

checklist.item: Warm layer (it gets cold at altitude)

campingSpots.name: Wadi Qadaah floor
campingSpots.notes: Wide flat section with mountain views on three sides.

tips: Temperatures at altitude can be 10°C cooler than the coast — pack accordingly.
The paved Jebel Jais road is a convenient evacuation route in emergencies.
Early morning offers the best light for photography in the canyon.
hazards: Falling rocks on steep canyon walls.
Cold nights in winter; hypothermia risk if camping unprepared.
Tight turns on narrow ledge tracks with drop-offs.

routes.name: Al Qudra Desert Loop
routes.summary: A popular desert loop in the Al Qudra conservation reserve south of Dubai, threading between camel tracks, the famous man-made lakes, and the Bab Al Shams dune belt. Ideal for beginners and families wanting a taste of desert driving close to the city.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 recommended; SUV with sand mode adequate on marked tracks
routes.permitInfo: No permit required. Keep to conservation zone tracks — off-track driving is restricted.

campingSpots.name: Al Qudra Lakes shore
campingSpots.notes: Popular overnight spot; flamingos and waterfowl often visible at dawn.

tips: The cycle track runs parallel — watch for cyclists at crossings.
Arrive at the lakes at sunrise for the best wildlife sightings.
Park near the Bab Al Shams signage to find the popular soft-sand dune entry.
hazards: Other vehicles and cyclists sharing the space.
Soft sand pockets near the lake edge can trap low-clearance vehicles.

routes.name: Mleiha Desert Dunes
routes.summary: Rolling red-sand dunes surrounding the UNESCO-associated Mleiha Archaeological Centre. The combination of ancient history and excellent dune terrain makes this unique — spend the morning exploring 210,000 years of human history and the afternoon in the dunes.
routes.permitInfo: Mleiha Archaeological Centre entry: AED 30 per adult. Dune area beyond is open access.

campingSpots.name: Mleiha dune camp
campingSpots.notes: Well-used site with excellent stargazing away from city lights.

tips: Book the guided archaeological tour in advance — combined culture-and-dunes days sell out in winter.
The centre has a cafe; stock up on water before heading into the dunes.
Dunes south-west of the centre are softer and more technical.
hazards: Dunes steepen significantly 5+ km south of the centre.
Occasional buggy and ATV rentals in the same area — share the terrain carefully.

routes.name: Tal Mireb / Empty Quarter Edge
routes.summary: A day-exploration of the dramatic northern escarpment of the Empty Quarter, accessible from the Liwa Crescent. Towering orange dunes up to 150 m, deep inter-dune valleys, and near-total silence make this one of the most awe-inspiring areas in the UAE.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 low-range; sand tyres essential; winch highly recommended
routes.groupSize: 3+ vehicles with lead driver experienced in Empty Quarter
routes.permitInfo: None; inform RAK Police or Abu Dhabi Civil Defence of your plan for remote expeditions.

campingSpots.name: Empty Quarter rim camp
campingSpots.notes: Epic 360-degree dune panorama; very cold at night in Dec–Jan.

tips: Never go alone and always share a GPS track with someone outside the group before departing.
Dunes here change shape after every windstorm — never rely on a track older than 2 weeks.
The journey from Abu Dhabi via Hameem takes ~4 hours; factor this into your day plan.
hazards: Extreme remoteness — rescue services are hours away.
Orientation is very difficult once deep in the dune sea.
No potable water; every drop must be carried.
Saudi border proximity — do not deviate south.

routes.name: Wadi Wurayah — Fujairah
routes.summary: The UAE's first designated mountain protected area spans 31,000 acres of rugged wadi terrain between Masafi, Khor Fakkan and Bidyah. The main wadi track threads through towering rock walls to seasonal waterfalls and freshwater pools — a lush contrast to the country's desert interior.
routes.vehicleReq: 4x4 with high clearance and low-range; protect underbody from submerged rocks
routes.permitInfo: Wadi Wurayah is a protected national park — entry is permitted but off-track driving is strictly prohibited. Camp only at designated spots.

checklist.item: Snorkel / wading gear for pool crossings

campingSpots.name: Lower wadi acacia grove
campingSpots.notes: Shaded by tall acacia trees; morning birdsong is spectacular.

campingSpots.name: Waterfall pool camp
campingSpots.notes: Near the seasonal waterfall; magical in spring after rain.

tips: Visit in February–March for the best chance of flowing waterfalls.
The Arabian tahr (mountain goat) is resident here — move quietly and you may spot one.
Fujairah municipality rangers may ask for ID at busy weekends; be cooperative.
hazards: Flash flooding risk during and after rain — the wadi can fill very quickly.
Submerged rocks at water crossings; wade on foot first before driving.
Wildlife protection rules — do not disturb animals or remove plants.
